#1963. Newcastle vs Arsenal: Team news, predicted line-ups and match preview

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal will have a tough task on hand as they visit St James’ Park.

Mikel Arteta’s side are five points clear at the top of the Premier League after their 1-0 victory over Hull City ahead of the international break. The Gunners have now gone nine games unbeaten in all competitions.

Despite only one win in their last six games, Newcastle will be a dangerous side at home.

Although Arsenal have won the last three encounters with Newcastle, recent games at Tyneside have not gone entirely smoothly for Mikel Arteta. He will also have to make a few key decisions in the squad with players injured and a busy run of fixtures.

Bruno Guimaraes will certainly be a topic of discussion for this game. The midfielder joined Newcastle four-and-a-half years ago, playing an important role in the development of the side, before moving to Arsenal on a reported 75 million pound move in the summer.

Whilst he has struggled to make himself an automatic starter in Arteta’s side, he could have a bigger impact with the absence of Martin Zubimendi.

Zubimendi is likely to be out for several weeks. Declan Rice should start, and Guimaraes is also likely to be involved, to form a double pivot.

Newcastle will try to play a gritty game to unsettle Arsenal. Despite Guimaraes’ knowledge of the opposition, he will have to assist the visitors to maintain control of the midfield battle.

Saliba is now back in contention after recovering from a back injury. The Frenchman has not played in the first team this season, but has made two appearances as he recovers. He played 45 minutes for the U21s.

Arteta confirmed that Saliba is in good shape and will begin to play more games, though he is unlikely to be in the starting line-up for the game against Newcastle.

Konsa should be in the starting line-up alongside Gabriel. Saliba could come on from the bench, as he looks to make his first competitive appearance of the season after the Champions League final last time out.

Saka is still unavailable due to quad trouble, whilst Dowman is suspended. Madueke should start on the right and Havertz will spearhead the attack.

Newcastle United: Predicted line-up not confirmed in the supplied team news.

Arsenal: Raya; Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Calafiori; Rice, Guimaraes; Madueke, Odegaard, Tzolis; Havertz.

Arsenal absentees: Martin Zubimendi, Bukayo Saka and Max Dowman.

Saliba is available but is not expected to start.

Newcastle have leaked goals at home this season. However, with Madueke and Tzolis providing pace in wide areas, this should not worry Arsenal too much.

Nevertheless, this game should be challenging for the Gunners. Newcastle are dangerous in attack and can capitalise on errors quickly in possession.

Despite Arsenal’s solid defensive record, they have failed to keep a clean sheet in their 4 visits to St James’ Park.

Overall this should be a good watch with goals scored by both sides. However, Arsenal should be able to pick up some vital 3 points.

Predicted score: Newcastle United 2-3 Arsenal.

#1962. Romano states Milan could be an option for Balde with Mendes links: “Discuss a strategy”

According to Fabrizio Romano, AC Milan could be involved in the market for Alejandro Balde once again this winter.

A central defender would be the main target for most Milan fans ahead of the winter mercato, but the possibility of signing another wing-back wouldn’t be turned down. In fact, with the left-side still proving to be a puzzling area, someone may need to be recruited.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

In the past, Balde has been linked and there have been several other suggestions. However, the Spaniard may be the most accessible mid-way through the season and it would seem that the Rossoneri are considering him again.

Speaking on his YouTube channel, Romano looked at the left-back’s future and didn’t deny that the Diavolo could be involved for another mercato, as MilanNews relayed.

“In the last few hours, Barcelona’s sporting director Deco spoke about Alejandro Balde and said that they are not planning on Balde’s exit because we are only in mid-November; there is a month and a half to go until January.

“Barça play every two or three days and a player like Balde can clearly still be useful between now and the transfer market. It’s true that Barça has left-back cover at the moment, but Barça doesn’t want to put a player like Balde on the market publicly already in mid-November.

“The reality behind the scenes is different: Balde remains a player who could leave in January, because Jorge Mendes, the player’s agent, was in Barcelona this week to speak with the player and discuss a strategy.

“Balde could therefore leave, but we must be realistic because there are significant figures at stake, given that he earns more than €5 million net and in the summer Barcelona were asking for €50 million for him.

“We’ll see if the formula can change in January, but on the one hand, Deco says so, on the other, there’s the reality: if Balde doesn’t play as well as he hasn’t been playing between now and January, the idea of ​​Balde leaving could become concrete.

“We told you that he’s currently being offered to Roma, but the Giallorossi haven’t really picked up steam yet. They’ve also offered him to Milan; the player was initially proposed last summer, but without a transfer, nothing happened.

“We’ll see what happens with Alejandro Balde, but he’s a name for the international or possibly Italian market that we need to keep there.”

Considering Sankhoun Diawara is now being considered as a left-back, the situation is certainly not ideal. So, Milan could certainly do worse than signing Balde.

#1961. West Ham 1 – 1 Preston North End | Player ratings as Parker drops more points

West Ham again conceded in the first half and spent the rest of the game peppering Preston’s goal – four efforts hit the woodwork but to no avail until Mavropanos’ second half equaliser. A lack of clinical finishing cost Scott Parker’s side dear as the points were shared.

Encouraging early touches with his feet and a willingness to catch rather than punch initially inspired confidence. Failed to get his fists to a corner, the ball striking Piroe on the head and looping over Herrick to give Preston a simple goal to create their lead. A superb double save just before half-time kept West Ham in touch after Mayers’ poor header. Grew in stature in the second half, notably catching balls where Hermansen might have punched.

Good early interplay with Bowen down the right. Unlucky not to score when his effort crashed against the post immediately after Bowen had hit the woodwork. Replaced by Souček on 78 minutes.

Solid enough first half without really being tested. Slipped in to meet a deflected Engels cross and equalise in true Mavropanos style.

Looked far more comfortable in the combative centre-back role, without being seriously tested for pace. Met Solomon’s second half cross with a header that was blocked.

Solid enough first half until a dreadful defensive header gifted the ball back to Preston, with Herrick rescuing him through a superb double save. Booked after misjudging his control and pulling down an opponent. Replaced by Scarles on 78 minutes.

A great through ball released Piroe for West Ham’s first decent opportunity. Excellent work out wide, crossing with his weaker foot to allow Mavropanos to equalise. Lots of wide running in a much more advanced position than under Nuno. Looked better for it.

Making his first appearance of the season, showed little sign of rustiness. Should have equalised after a well-worked corner, curling into the side-netting. Looked increasingly at home sitting in front of the defence and moving remarkably quickly across the turf. Quick feet in the opposition box led to a shot poked agonisingly close, but just wide. A pretty good shift on his return; surprising he lasted until 90 minutes, when Magassa replaced him.

Should have taken a first-time shot with his right foot, but instead shifted onto his favoured left and scuffed the chance in the first half. Needs to produce more. Evidently Parker agrees as he was replaced by Castellanos on 57 minutes.

Struck the post with a right-footed effort as West Ham pressed for an equaliser. Had the beating of his full-back in the second half, making frequent runs down the right and crossing with his weaker foot. Several shots but lacked that killer punch – as did the whole attack.

Should have opened the scoring after ten minutes when sent through one-on-one by Engels, but the goalkeeper saved. Lots of trying and ‘nearlies’ but too little output. Booked on 82 minutes for a professional foul. Not enough from the striker.

A decent early effort from 25 yards went straight at the goalkeeper. Immediately after the restart, stepped inside and struck the bar with a brilliant curling right-footed shot. Replaced by Solomon on 57 minutes at which point West Ham’s pace and zip largely vanished. There’s a lesson in there…

On for Austbø, 57 minutes. One jinking run inside produced a cross met by Morato’s head, but the effort was blocked. Looked very right-footed and unable to beat defenders on the outside. West Ham were poorer for the substitution of Austbø and Solomon’s introduction.

On for Mukasa, 57 minutes. Fluffed his lines on 85 minutes, looping a back-post header over the bar.

On for Mayers, 78 minutes. One decent cross late on. Understandably rusty-looking.

On for Veltman, 78 minutes. Almost won it in the 94th minute with a back-post header tipped over by Preston’s goalkeeper.

#1960. West Ham 1 – 1 Preston | Final score, first impression as more points slip away

West Ham’s familiar profligacy in front of goal came back to haunt them, as did their propensity to go behind in the first half of games as the points were shared at London Stadium this afternoon.

From Preston’s first corner, the fanbase was understandably apprehensive, knowing West Ham’s weaknesses from dead balls earlier in the season. Again the curse struck, with Piroe heading the ball over his own oncoming goal keeper’s fists, the ball then looping onto the post and allowing a gentle tap-in for Preston to take the lead.

Herrick rallied well after conceding early

The wheels could have come off for West Ham’s young goal keeper at that point: However, all credit to Herrick. It would have been very easy for his confidence to crumble after that early combi-cock-up, but he rallied well and even appeared to be smiling as the game went on, with several catches and a couple of really good saves surely meaning the shirt is his for the time being.

West Ham hit the post four times during a frenetic period in the first half when their intensity was high, but it seemed as though the ball simply would not go between the posts.

Familiar problems surfaced in the second half as the pace dropped and West Ham ran out of ideas, notably after Austbø had been substituted. Manor Solomon, looking very one-footed, simply ran inside and passed square. Frustratingly, the game slowed in pace in the last twenty minutes with the Hammers looking devoid of new ideas just at the time when they should have been upping the tempo.

It is clear that there’s still a shortage of pace in this side and with a build up that got slower as the game went on, West Ham’s bench looked as if it desperately needed an injection of Antonio-like pace to scare opponents and perhaps take on a shot!

A disappointment for the West Ham supporters, who booed their team off in the now time-honoured tradition as another two points went west. Against the bottom side.

#1959. Scott Parker tells us there are positives – but talk is cheap | West Ham News

West Ham failed to overcome bottom side Preston North End in what was a desperately disappointing spectacle for West Ham fans who had been expecting so much more from their new manager’s first home game.

A scrappy first goal conceded came from pretty much Preston’s only attempt at goal, and then our visitors sat back in time-honoured tradition.  Four times the Hammers crashed the ball against the woodwork in a first half which showed plenty of promise, however the second half evaporated in familiar fashion, inexplicably, no sooner than Mavropanos crashed in the equaliser.

Just about every fan expected West Ham to go on and win the game convincingly – yet instead they huffed and puffed with endless ‘after you – no after you’ short, sideways passes as nobody took responsibility for making the killer pass or – heaven forbid- taking on the shot.

However, the West Ham manager will no doubt do his best, tomorrow maybe, to pull out positives, despite being ‘devastated‘ at the result:

Edson Álvarez, in his first game this season, El Machin was, surprisingly, up to speed pretty much immediately, sitting in front of the defence. He was everywhere: collecting, tidying up, harrying, attacking and breaking down opponents’ attacks. The late-tackling liability of last season was nowhere to be seen as he impressed and looks as if he has found himself a role for the coming weeks.

However, there’s a caveat: Remember this is the bottom side in the division who have just held us to draw. It will be intriguing to see if he copes against tougher opponents.

Edson Alvarez -Looked in control this afternoon – of his own discipline and of his midfield patch.

Finn Herrick: It can only have been unsettling, as the young keeper came to punch his first corner only to find a team mate’s glancing header got there first, looping the ball over his outstretched fists and allowing Preston to open the scoring against the run of play.

Credit to him, Herrick kept his cool and grew in stature as the game went on. He made an excellent double save after Mayers’ poor defensive header, and played well with the ball at his feet, combining Areola’s shot-stopping ability and Hermansen’s football skills.

However, positives aside, Parker has his work cut out simply to get this team’s work rate up. This time, they started quick and could have had three in the first half, even though there was a hesitancy and a lack of creation in front of goal.

Why it evaporated no sooner than the Hammers had equalised was a mystery. What should have become a barrage launched on Preston’s goal became a last thirty minutes of frustrating misfiring.

Just. Not. Good.Enough. Despite the bright points which Parker referenced in his post – match conference.

Just don’t blame West Ham’s newest manager for the failure of the last three to demand pacy, attacking football and recruiting so-called strikers who wouldn’t have made it into West Ham’s championships side of 2004/5 or 2011/12.

Can’t make a silk purse out of a sows ear. Especially not in two weeks.

Nick Woltemade was left out of the Juventus starting eleven on Sunday.

After a woeful goalless opening half Juventus were booed off the pitch.

Nick Woltemade introduced for the start of the second half and the rest is history.

Within 14 minutes Juventus had the game won.

Nick Woltemade scoring the opening goal within eight minutes of entering the pitch.

It was then 2-0 within 14 minutes as the Newcastle United loan star got the assist for Teun Koopmeiners.

Juan Cabal a third goal, before then Nick Woltemade passed up the chance of scoring his second when he handed the ball to fellow striker Randal Kolo Muani to score from the penalty spot.

A goalless first half shocker transformed into a thumping second half 4-0 Juventus triumph.

Supersub Nick Woltemade handed the man of the match trophy after the final whistle.

When Sports Dunia reported on the match. they waxed lyrical about the contribution of Nick Woltemade: ‘Came on and instantly changed the game. His close-range finish for the opener broke Venezia’s resistance and shifted all momentum. We noticed his intelligent movement between lines, dragging defenders out of shape. He also assisted Koopmeiners, showing composure in the box. From our perspective, a superb super-sub performance.’

Nick Woltemade has still only started seven games in all competitions for Juventus but now has eight direct goal contributions, scoring five and getting three assists.

#1957. West Ham 1-1 Preston: Scott Parker Still Struggling To Unlock Jarrod Bowen

West Ham were nowhere near good enough against the worst team in the division. Whilst we had our chances, it would be a long stretch to suggest we were significantly better than Preston, particularly during a first half in which the visitors created opportunities of their own.

Edson Álvarez looked decent enough on his return to the team, but Scott Parker looks no closer to getting the best out of Jarrod Bowen than Nuno Espírito Santo or Graham Potter did. In essence, the Hammers lacked magic, and watching our best player pinned to the right flank was depressing.

The statistics certainly make for interesting reading. West Ham registered 30 attempts on goal, but only four were on target. We also hit the woodwork three times, with Bowen and Joël Veltman striking opposite posts during the same passage of play before Edvin Austbø rattled the crossbar shortly after half-time.

Preston took the lead through Liam Lindsay after just 18 minutes, following a corner which Joël Piroe inadvertently flicked towards his own goal.

Konstantinos Mavropanos eventually equalised on the hour mark, heading home Arne Engels’ cross after Manor Solomon had helped create the opening.

Yet even after drawing level, West Ham couldn’t find a winner against a team who arrived at the London Stadium bottom of the Championship.

There were chances, certainly. Tomáš Souček had a late header tipped over, while Mavropanos headed over in stoppage time. But for all the possession and pressure, there was precious little composure in front of goal.

And as far as I’m concerned, this was a match West Ham simply had to win.

What makes the situation particularly frustrating is that we’ve already seen what Bowen can do when he’s given more freedom.

During the remarkable comeback against Cardiff City, our captain was allowed to drift into central positions, where he caused all sorts of problems. His movement, passing and ability to find space helped transform a game which had looked completely lost at half-time.

I was so impressed that I subsequently wrote about how Scott Parker needed to restore West Ham’s most dangerous weapon.

Unfortunately, against Blackburn, Bowen was back operating as a conventional right winger. And against Preston, we saw much the same thing.

That’s not to suggest Bowen didn’t contribute. He was involved throughout and managed eight attempts on goal, including the effort which struck the post.

But there’s a difference between getting Bowen involved in the game and getting the best out of him.

West Ham have spent far too long relying on our captain to produce something special from wide positions, often with defenders able to anticipate where he’s going to receive the ball.

Against Cardiff, we briefly saw something different.

Bowen was the inspiration behind that second-half recovery. He looked far more dangerous when he was able to move into the middle and influence the game rather than remaining tied to the touchline.

I genuinely thought Parker had stumbled upon something which could change West Ham’s season.

Instead, two matches later, we seem to have gone backwards.

Of course, the manager has plenty of other issues demanding his attention.

There were some positives against Preston. Álvarez made his first Championship appearance for West Ham since May 2025 and looked reasonably comfortable in midfield, while young goalkeeper Finlay Herrick produced an excellent double save to prevent the visitors doubling their lead.

Mavropanos also deserves credit for another important goal, particularly given that he is a centre-back who continues to contribute at the other end of the pitch.

But the bigger picture remains deeply concerning.

West Ham simply had to start turning the London Stadium into somewhere opposition teams feared visiting.

Instead, the bottom club have come away with a point, and Parker has now overseen two draws and a defeat in his first three matches.

I appreciate he hasn’t been in the job long, and I’m not suggesting he’s solely responsible for problems which have been developing for some considerable time.

However, the international break gave him an opportunity to work with the players, and I had hoped to see considerably more improvement than we witnessed.

For me, the biggest concern remains our inability to get the best out of Bowen.

We have a player capable of providing the creativity, movement and unpredictability that this team so desperately needs. Yet we’re still asking him to spend most of his time playing in the same predictable areas of the pitch.

West Ham don’t lack effort. Against Preston, they certainly didn’t lack possession or attempts on goal.

And until Scott Parker finds a way of giving Jarrod Bowen the freedom to provide it, I fear we’re going to see plenty more afternoons like this one.

The only place to start is the way that the team responded after the break.

Were these two players signed as first teamers for this season?

I’ve seen reports saying that the manager is calling for more recruitment in January. It’s all a bit baffling.

#1954. Newcastle United Game Management issue is huge Red Herring

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The issue of Newcastle United Game Management has reared its head once again.

It always hurts when you take the lead and end up drawing, or even worse, lose.

Especially if it is a late goal that is conceded.

After the 2-2 draw with Arsenal, I have heard and read a fair few fans questioning the Newcastle United Game Management.

What these fans are questioning, is basically whyafter coming back to lead against Arsenal with 62 minutes on the clock, why couldn’t Matthias Jaissle and his players see out the rest of the match without conceding?

The 3 positives and 3 negatives piece on The Mag this Monday morning perfectly summed up the kind of thing I have been seeing.

David Punton selecting ‘Game Management’ as one of his three negatives and saying: ‘Another winning position has been thrown away. The same thing happened down at Fulham. It drives you crackers at times. They surely must have to work on how to see a game out? It’s not rocket science.’

So is this true, the Newcastle United Game Management a huge issue?

First of all I have had a look at the 14 Newcastle United matches this season from purely a statistical viewpoint.

Do Newcastle United repeatedly take the lead and throw it away?

Newcastle United when scoring the opening goal of the game this season, what ended up the final result? Won 4 (Spurs, Millwall, Hull, Palace), Drawn 2 (Liverpool, Fulham) Lost 0

Newcastle United when conceding the opening goal of the game this season, what ended up the final result? Won 1 (West Brom), Drawn 2 (Bournemouth, Arsenal) Lost 5 (Leeds, Coventry, Villa, Everton x2)

Which matches have Newcastle United scored the final goal of the game? Happened seven times (West Brom, Spurs, Bournemouth, Millwall, Leeds, Palace, Everton cup)

Which matches have Newcastle United conceded the final goal of the game? Happened seven times (Liverpool, Hull, Coventry, Villa, Everton, Fulham, Arsenal)

In his Positives and Negatives piece, David Punton says about the supposed failings of Newcastle United Game Management: ‘They surely must have to work on how to see a game out? It’s not rocket science.’

I am not just having a go at David here but what exactly is this magical way of ensuring that there is zero chance of allowing the opposition to score once you have taken the lead?

Newcastle United went 2-1 up on 62 minutes, so Arsenal had what turned out to be 37 minutes to get an equaliser (and then potential winner…).

They are the best team in the Premier League and have the strongest bench.

What is the absolute certain route to not letting them score?

As the stats show above, Newcastle United have given as good as they have got this season when it comes to scoring first and the eventual result, compared to the games when the opposition have scored first.

If you are leading by a single goal and it is the last minute of a match, then all your defenders recklessly charge up the pitch and you concede, that would be really poor Newcastle United Game Management.

It would be really poor Newcastle United Game Management if leading and then gifted an equaliser when trying a daft risky pass on the edge of your own penalty area.

This didn’t happen on Saturday, nor indeed at Fulham in the previous match.

Arsenal scored with 21 minutes left to play when some excellent play got them up the pitch and Madueke scored a good goal, which even though it went through a Newcastle defender’s legs you think Lukas Hornicek should have saved it.

Newcastle scored in the 80th minute at Craven Cottage and Fulham had to throw everything at them, they got the benefit of a bit of a scramble in our penalty area and two deflections contributed to their equaliser.

This isn’t disastrous Newcastle United Game Management, this is football.

It is a huge Red Herring to claim this is a serious problem this season for Matthias Jaissle and his team.

#1953. Chelsea’s feisty friendly ends in penalty shoot-out confusion

Chelsea’s Far East tour ended in farce and confusion with players waiting around for a penalty shoot-out that never happened.

The chaos came at the end of a hard-earned, bad-tempered draw against Malaysian champions Johor Darul Ta’zim, with an own-goal in the 89th minute sparring the west London side’s blushes.

That goal also was supposed to set up penalties. But after minutes of waiting around – and Kevin Campello, Chelsea’s head of first-team operations, saying “it’s written in the contract” – the players walked off the pitch.

That confusion ended a feisty affair in which tensions threatened to boil over and that, at certain points, paid little attention to the “friendly” aspect of the clash with seven yellow cards shown. At one point the visitors’ new set-piece coach Austin MacPhee exchanged angry words with some of Johor’s coaching staff. The CFC TV commentary team suggested that the spot-kicks were abandoned because of the match’s heated atmosphere.

Austin MacPhee was ready to throw hands😂 pic.twitter.com/CFDgTOwmxE

Having played just 24 hours earlier in Jakarta – a 3-0 win over AC Milan – it was no surprise to see Xabi Alonso name a fresh XI, a mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters given much-needed game time.

And considering Johor are one game away from setting a new world record of 109 matches unbeaten in the top flight – a run that would surpass the current mark set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s – it was also no shock to see the Malaysian team offer a stern, pre-season test for the west Londoners.

After a good start Chelsea were second best in a first half in which Johor should have been at least two goals to the good. The Malaysian champions controlled the first 45 minutes and were 1-0 up after 14 minutes – a low cross from the left side-footed home by Arif Aiman.

The hosts gave the young, inexperienced Chelsea backline a torrid time, especially on the flanks and Óscar Arribas was guilty of not capitalising on a great chance to double Johor’s lead, his shot after cutting in from the right going wide.

While they looked vulnerable at the back, Chelsea also struggled to keep possession in attack. But they got an equaliser they scarcely deserved after Liam Delap was manhandled to the ground in the box by Kevin Medina. The striker, who may well leave Stamford Bridge before the transfer window slams shut, fired home the spot-kick allowing the visitors to go into the break on level terms.

For the most part, the second half followed a similar pattern to the first – Jofor having the better chances, while tensions on the pitch continued to run high.

It was, however, Chelsea who took the lead after the break, Delap once again scoring from the spot, this time after Jamie Gittens was brought down in the area.

Johor, though, kept on creating, thanks in part to a fairly porous visitors’ backline, and levelled through a deflected Arribas free kick, before going 3-2 up thanks thanks to a well-taken Bérgson strike.

Had it stayed that way Chelsea could have had few complaints. But as the clock approached 90 minutes, the visitors had one last attack. Mykhailo Mudryk, just on as a substitute, delivered a cross from the left that Antonio Glauder could only steer into his own net. That was supposed to set up the penalty shoot-out that did not take place and the chance for one of the sides to claim a hollow victory.

Considering a raft of changes and that fact this was far from the first XI, it is hard to know what to make of this. But among the positive things Alonso could take from the game was the impressive form of Nicolas Jackson and good centre-forward play of Delap. The negative was, however, a poor defensive display.

Chelsea return to Stamford Bridge on Saturday for their last pre-season friendly, against Real Sociedad, before the Premier League season starts away at local rivals Fulham on August 24.

Johor Darul Ta’zim: Syihan Hazmi; Arribas, Israfilov (Carlos Akapo 82), Medina, Antonio Glauder, Silva (La’Vere Corbin-Ong 89); Arif Aiman, Petrovic, Méndez (Nené 78), Marcos Guilherme (Bérgson); Zahedi (Stoichkov 62). Substitutes: Abad, Davies, Hidalgo, Nahuel Leiva, Lowry, Mohamadou Sumareh, Stuart Wilkin.Booked: Israfilov, Antonio Glauder, Silva.Goals: Arif Aiman (14), Arribas (65), Bérgson (86).Chelsea: Sharman-Lowe (Slolina 46); Subuloye, Adarabioyo, Anselmino (Watson 29); Geovany Quenda, Dario Essugo, Nicoll-Jazuli, Gittens (Mudryk 87); Estêvão, Delap, Jacskon (Satpaev 86). Substitutes: Curd, Diakite, Kavuma-McQueen, Sarr, Walsh.Booked: Estêvão, Delap, Jackson, Geovany Quenda, Watson.Goals: Delap (42 pen, 62 pen), Antonio Glauder (89 og).

There will NOT be a penalty shootout. No one is quite sure why.

Anyway, that was an entertaining draw, plenty of good things for Chelsea (the play of Delap and Jackson) as well as worrying signs (open and vulnerable at the back).

The commentators on CFC TV are now not so sure!

That was an entertaining pre-season friendly. There was a bit of niggle and that added to the action.

There will be penalties, apparently, if it stays the same score...

Will there be a late winner? There will be four minutes of added time.

Mudryk just on picks up the ball on the left and, with four Chelsea players in the box, crosses into the danger area. It’s a good ball and asks too many questions of the hosts as Glauder diverts the ball into his own net.

It’s what the host have, on the balance of play, deserved, but it’s a gift from Chelsea. Essugo loses the ball in the final third and Bergson, on as sub pick it put driving at the box before hitting a low shot from outside the area, the ball nestling in the left corner of the net.

Chelsea have been better this half than the first 45, they’ve been able to control the pace of the game well since the break.

The pace has slowed down since the break, Chelsea seeing more of the ball. They work it right before Watson loses possession on the edge of the area.

The referee clearly forgot about the hydration break and the two teams are having a belated one now. Delightful...

I reckon there’s another goal left in this match. It’s been entertaining fare and the hosts have given as good as they’ve got, if not more.

This has been a lively match, better than most run-of-the-mill pre-season friendlies. Chelsea seeing a fair bit of possession at the moment, can they fashion a chance?

Yes they can. But it’s a longish shot from Gittens that is easily saved by Hamzi in the JDT goal.

More niggle in this match that hasn’t really had many tough challenges. After a few handbags the referee takes control and the argy bargy peters out.

It’s the least the hosts deserve. They have a free-kick 25 yards out, Arribas takes it with his right it’s at the wall but in turning away from the ball Delap deflects it into the far-right corner giving Slonina no chance.

Fluky goal but the hosts have deserved their bit of luck.

Delap again with the goal, this time he goes low, but still to the keeper’s right.

Penalty for Chelsea. Gittens cuts back in the box onto his right and is clipped by the defender. Clear-cut penalty.

Half-chance for Delap on the edge of the area. He playes a one-two with Jackson before opening up his body and letting fly, the shot going well wide.

Another good chance for the hosts and it’s not shock to write that it’s come from the industry of Arribas on the right. He fires in a low cross that evades everyone in the box.

Estevao goes down in the box, it looks as though it could well be a penalty but the referee waves play on. The Brazilian is the shown a yellow card for possibly lashing out having not got the decision he wanted.

The hosts have asserted themselves well this half, in much the same way as they did in the first 45 minutes.

Another good chance for the hosts and again it’s all too easy as Zahedi is one-on-one with the keeper. The striker, however, dithers a bit too long and Slonina makes a fine save. JDT have had plenty of chances to add to their sole goal...

Chelsea have had a ragged start to this half.

Good work from JDT who keep the ball well in midfield before a throughball is played to the on-rushing Zahedi but Slonina comes out well.

They’re back under way in Johor, and there’s an early chance for Jackson who gets the ball in the box, but the ball gets stuck underneath him and he cannot get in a good attempt in on goal.

And that is the last action of an entertaining half. Chelsea started well before the hosts opened the scoring. JDT then took control of the half and should, if truth be told, have extended their lead. But Delap did well to earn the penalty that he subsequently scored and should have made it 2-1 with the last kick of the 45.

Worrying signs at the back, however, for Alonso. Will Chelsea go to four at the back after the break?

The answer to that question (see last post) was so very nearly yes...

Jackson plays in a peach of a through ball with the outside of his right foot, Delap is one-on-one with the keeper and looks for all the world as though he has to score. BUT he scuffs his shot wide.

There will be three minutes of added time. Can Chelsea head into the break with an unexpected lead?

Free-kick for Chelsea on the JDT byline. The ball is put deep into the box, it’s headed back by Tosin before the ball is blazed over the bar.

A minute later Tosin then let’s fly form 25 yards, the ball goes well over the bar.

The hosts should have been more than 1-0 to the good and now they’re drawing. Goals change matches...

Having won the penalty Delap fires the spotkick home, sending the keeper the the wrong way.

Penalty to Chelsea and it’s all thanks to good centre-forward play by Delap. He gets the ball in the box and Medina manhands him to the ground. The referee doesn’t hesitate before pointing to the spot.

Chelsea have struggled to create anything since the opening 15 minutes. They have no control at the front and none at the back currently.

As I type that JDT have another good chance to turn the 1-0 lead into a 2-0 lead. Arribas, whose been a menace all game, dances toward the Chelsea box before delaying the pass too long.

JDT are finding a lot of joy on the flanks, there are three at the back for Chelsea and on the outside are two youngsters. The hosts are working the space well.

Yet again Chelsea are made to look decidedly average. A simple ball over the top on the right opens up the visitors’ defence and Arribas is in on goal, he cuts in and lets fly with his left peg, the shot going wide.

That should have been 2-0 to the Malaysian powerhouses.

Worrying signs for Chelsea who have struggled to keep possession up top and looked vulnerable at the back.

Yet more good work from JDT who are being given space by Chelsea. Marcos Guilherme slaloms into the west Londoners’ box and Tosin again doesn’t look the most assured but the JDT player cuts the ball back and the visitors can clear the danger.

Another good attack from the hosts who get in a shot in on goal, it’s deflected and loops into the grateful arms of Sharman-Lowe in the Chelsea goal.

There’s a break in play with Anselmino down and suffering what looks like a hamstring injury. He is eventually replaced by Reggie Watson.

Meanwhile, the home fans are in fine voice and waving several HUGE flags.

Yep, everyone’s least favourite part of the World Cup in the U, S of A is back. To be fair it’s humid in Johor so taking on fluids during the first 45 minutes is no bad idea.

There’s a bit of argy-bargy not really what you should get in a ‘friendly’. There hasn’t been a bad chellenge in the match so far so not sure where that came from...

Yet more good work from the hosts, this time it’s down the right, Arribas getting the better of Anselmino before shooting at the near post - the attempt hitting the side netting.

After a lively start Chelsea have been second best.

Poor defending from the visitors there but the chance was well snapped up by JDT.

Lovely break from the hosts. They break down the left at pace, before the ball is threaded through to the back post and Arif Aiman sidefoots into the back of the net with aplomb.

So very nearly an opener for Chelsea. They break at pace thanks to Estevao who drives down the middle before playing in Jackson. The striker cuts in from the left and shoots, the attempt is saved well by Hamzi and Estevao’s follow up is wide. Is a goal coming?

Free-kick for Chelsea some 35 yards out. Too far fro a shot on goal? Of course it is. The ball is floated into the box and the visitors earn a corner.

What can they create from this set piece? ‘Not much’ is the initial answer as the ball is cleared by JDT but Chelsea win possession back and the ball is fed to Estevao on the left, the Brazilian goes for go with his trusty left peg but the bal goes high and wide.

JDT attack down the left, it’s a lovely ball in that forces a fine header to clear the danger from Adarabioyo.

No sooner had I sent that last post than Chelsea break through the middle. The ball is fed through to Delap who gets a left-footed shot in on goal forcing a good save from the JDT keeper Hamzi.

Quiet, low-key start to the match. No real shock there, it is a pre-season friendly.

JDT give the ball away in their half and Chelsea have a half-decent platform to launch an attack from. They cannot fashion a chance and also lose possession.

They’re under way in southern Malaysia, Chelsea are in their vibrant blue and the hosts are wearing a fetching pink number. There was a late change for the visitors, Mamadou Sarr has been replaced by Olutayo Subuloye.

CHELSEA XI TO FACE JOHOR: Sharman-Lowe; Sarr, Tosin, Anselmino; Quenda, Nicoll-Jazuli, Essugo (c), Gittens; Estevao; Jackson, Delap; subs: Slonina, Curd, Subuloye, Diakite, Watson, Mudryk, Walsh, Kavuma-McQueen, Satpayev

...Luis Garcia. The Spaniard has history with Chelsea, remember the ‘ghost goal’?

Arriving for duty! 🫡 pic.twitter.com/M2XEkLC18n

Your Chelsea side today! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/0OvvGVmgpc

A mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters you may not have heard of.

Johor Darul Ta’Zim – more commonly known as JDT – are the Man Utd of Malaysia (at least that’s according to a Malaysian friend of mine). In 2013, they were going nowhere and were the dictionary definition of a stagnant club, low on confidence and trophies. That was until the Crown Prince bought the club and, over the next 13 years, transformed it into the powerhouse it is today.

As if to underline JDT’s dominance over Malaysian football they are one game away from the world record unbeaten run in a top flight. The new season of the Malaysian Super League gets under way later this month and should they avoid defeat in their opening match they will extend their unbeaten run - which began in April 2021 - to 109 games and surpass the world record set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s.

Chelsea’s pre-season tour of South East Asia ends today with a match against Johor Darul Ta’zim in Malaysia. The clash comes barely 24 hours after the west Londoners beat AC Milan 3-0 in Jakarta, a much-needed win coming on the back of defeats against Juventus and Tottenham.

A fine volley from Moises Caicedo and a double from João Pedro either side of half-time led Xabi Alonso’s side to victory in the Indonesian capital.

The game was fairly even in the first half and looked set to head into the break level at 0-0 but Pedro’s header from Caicedo’s corner put Chelsea in front.

Alonso’s side then doubled their advantage seconds into the second half as Pedro scored his second, assisted by Pedro Neto.

Just minutes later, Chelsea had their third courtesy of a well-worked corner routine. Romeo Lavia’s delivery was met by Caicedo on the volley, with the Ecuadorian’s finish with the outside of the boot finding the bottom corner.

Today, the west London side face Malaysian powerhouses Johor at the Sultan Ibrahim Stadium, more on them later, but considering the tight turnaround from yesterday’s match today’s clash will provide a stern test.

“The idea, with the game against Milan and then one in Johor, was to arrive at this weekend with players not being ready for 90 minutes until now,” Alonso explained after the win in Jakarta.

“We wanted to have a logical progression in their loads; so we had our plan and we’ve stuck to that.

“We have another idea [against Johor]; that was decided yesterday [Friday]. The idea is that many young players were coming to have chances to play tomorrow. If not, we’d have been short, as playing two games in two days is quite intense. So we will need them.”

Stay here for all the team news and action with kick-off set for 1pm.

#1952. West Ham 1 – 1 Preston North End : The morning after

That eight point gap between West Ham United in tenth and the Championship front runners is starting to look mighty huge with just sixteen games completed.

Of course the reality is that there are still thirty games remaining but West Ham will have to find a way of converting all the huffing and puffing into points or else we will find ourselves scratching around even trying to make the enlarged play off places come May next year.

“Wasteful West Ham”: Not my words but the description on the official club web site which sums up perfectly an afternoon of toil and frustration against the bottom side in the league.

Scott Parker pronounced himself happy with the effort, if ‘bitterly disappointed’ with the result. As were we all.

The team announcement produced a wave of optimism, and I’m not sure yet that we should ditch that: Tenth place is not where we expected to be at the end of November but there is still plenty of time to turn the West Ham supertanker back on course and away from the rocky peril of mid table, second division mediocrity.

But three years’ decline won’t be fixed in three games.

Introducing Fin Herrick and Edson Alvarez were bold decisions which could have backfired totally, especially after the maddening concession in the first half. Now Scott Parker needs to keep his nerve and persevere with that set up, go again on Tuesday night away at Fratton Park and trust for better luck and better finishing.

Ninety points still up for grabs this season, Hammers.

At least the ownership saw fit to ditch Nuno in time to turn the ship around. In the bad old days of David Sullivan, we’d still be on about game 5 of 20 ‘must win’ games before Nuno had to walk the plank. (Not sure where all the nautical terms came from this morning).

In any case, there’s not another manager who’d do any better in Scott Parker’s place right now. Don’t panic. Yet. COYI!

From the old Bobby Moore Upper to the Billy Bonds' stand these days - I've been watching since '03 and a supporter since about 1970.. Favourite player - Dean Ashton: Curse you Shaun Wright-Phillips. I still watch YouTube repeats of the Cup Final of 2006 hoping in vain that Shaka Hislop grows another six inches and stops Steven Gerrard's injury time equaliser. Can tell I'm getting old knowing I watched both Mark Noble's debut and his last game at West Ham. Pulling on a Claret and Blue replica shirt still makes me feel the same butterflies as when I was seven years old. Magic.

The problem as I see it is in two areas. Firstly we are struggling at home. Is this the stadium and the supporters not begin close to the pitch to create the pressure on the opposition? Second is obviously the team itself. Scoring for the forward line seems to be an issue, this is glaringly obvious when a centre back is out Scoring the forward line. The best forward line we have was probably out yesterday and still didn’t score! This issue can be sorted in the January window but will that be quick enough, who knows. In the mean time I applaud the brave selection yesterday and hope the keeper keeps his place.

Weve got to be realistic We are no longer that supertanker of old WE are a rotting old barge rudderless We dont even own our own berth to dock into on stormy days

Oh by the way theres is a certain Michael Carrick out there available

Carrick’s success in the Championship pales in comparison to Parker’s. We are on the right horse.

Can’t see Michael Carrick replacing Mukasa any time soon Mick.

His best playing days are long, long gone.

Although I think he has the required coaching badges and so could replace Mark Noble in the background.

We’re caught in Groundhog Day watching the same game over and over again. We go behind and it can be one, two or even three behind, then we spend the rest of the match playing catch up which we often do but sometimes don’t.

It’s like we can’t rewrite the script so only the same thing ever happens.

Until something does change it we are where we are, we’re a mid-table Championship team.

Yesterday was particularly galling as we can’t even beat the bottom team at home. These are not good teams we’re struggling against.

Another year in the championship will do me fine, full house at the London Stadium, refs that don’t blow up everytime someone rolls round on the floor and no VAR. West Ham the football club will just have to cut its clothe accordingly. Buying Premier league players and retaining the ones who took us down, Bowen included, doesn’t make a great championship squad that gets you promoted. It needs a winning mentality, relegated players just don’t have what it takes.

The proverbial game of two halves for United and Arsenal.

Mikel Arteta’s side totally dominating the opening 45 minutes.

After the break it was Matthias Jaissle’s team that were by far the better side.

BBC Sport journalist Alex Howell giving these comments on the Newcastle United players and a rating for each.

Lukas Hornicek: His kicking was slightly erratic. Nearly got caught on the ball by Kai Havertz after taking too long to release it. Could have done better with the second Arsenal goal. 5 (Davey Hat-Trick 5)

Amar Dedic: Booked after pulling back Eberechi Eze and had a tough evening against the England forward. 5 (Davey Hat-Trick 4)

Malick Thiaw: Scored the goal to put Newcastle in front, which capped an excellent performance in central defence. 8 (Davey Hat-Trick 8)

Dan Burn: Some crucial clearances in the first half and played a big part as Newcastle took the lead. 7 (Davey Hat-Trick 8)

Lewis Hall: A big error for the opening goal when he failed to deal with a clipped ball over the top. The left back redeemed himself with a crucial block to deny Noni Madueke and provided some excellent deliveries into the Arsenal box. 7 (Davey Hat-Trick 6)

Joe Willock: An all-action performance and his physicality was a big reason why Newcastle improved in the second half. 7 (Davey Hat-Trick 6)

Harvey Barnes: An excellent finish to bring Newcastle level and was always direct. 8 (Davey Hat-Trick 8)

William Osula: Isolated as he led the Newcastle attack but did very well to assist his side’s opening goal. 7 (Davey Hat-Trick 6.5)

Anthony Elanga (on 46, Murphy): His pace meant Newcastle always had an option in behind. 6 (Davey Hat-Trick 5.5)

Jacob Ramsey (on 46, Steur): Added drive to the midfield. 7 (Davey Hat-Trick 6)

Sven Botman (on 92, Hall) (Davey Hat-Trick 5)

The BBC Sport journalist missed the fact that Yoane Wissa came on in the 83rd minute (Davey Hat-Trick 4)

#1950. Eddie Howe and Jason Tindall deliver ‘exclusive football masterclass’ at school and inspiring Q&A

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Nothing had been heard of Eddie Howe and Jason Tindall since their official departure from Newcastle United at the end of July.

Apart that is from endless speculation about where the duo might end up next.

Manchester United of course recently speculated as a likely destination for Eddie Howe (and presumably Jason Tindall and most of the rest of Howe’s NUFC backroom team).

Mauricio Pochettino has of course taken on that particular poisoned chalice at Man U (and got off to a great start at Anfield!).

The radio silence on Eddie Howe ended at the weekend and we covered it on The Mag. The former NUFC boss having moved back down to the south coast and Southampton manager Tonda Eckert revealed that Eddie Howe had visited the Saints’ training ground and they’d had a chat.

This has now quickly been followed by a school making public that both Eddie Howe and Jason Tindall have paid them a visit.

The pair visiting Bromley High School GDST, with the school giving a rundown of what happened on the day.

The school stating: ‘Bromley High School students were treated to an unforgettable day of top flight sport as former Newcastle United Manager Eddie Howe and Assistant Manager Jason Tindall visited the school to deliver an exclusive football masterclass and an inspiring Q&A session.’

A few snippets from their report of the day:

‘When asked what defines a great leader, Howe emphasised that leadership begins with personal standards rather than titles. He encouraged students to focus on everyday habits, such as being the first to arrive, the last to leave and treating peers with kindness and integrity. Howe told the students, noting that trustworthiness and consistency are what truly earn the respect of teammates and classmates. Tindall echoed this sentiment, adding that genuine leadership means supporting others and leading through actions rather than words.’

Navigating Pressure and Building Resilience

‘Students asked how top-flight managers handle team selection, media scrutiny, and setbacks. Howe explained that he and Tindall rely on honest, consistent processes, focusing on training effort and tactical preparation rather than outside noise. He also praised Tindall’s loyalty and behind-the-scenes support, highlighting how strong partnerships rely on trust and unity even when difficult decisions are made.

Discussing how athletes bounce back from mistakes, both coaches stressed the importance of blocking out social media negativity and leaning on trusted support networks, coaches, teammates, family and friends. Howe shared how breaking challenges down into simple, achievable steps helps players regain confidence, while Tindall noted how achieving major milestones can fuel lasting self-belief.’

‘In response to a question about player development, Howe shared examples of how dedication and adaptability pay off at the highest level, from players staying after training every day to perfect their technical skills to others successfully transitioning into entirely new positions on the pitch. Howe told the students natural talent must always be matched by a relentless work ethic and coachability.

The duo also highlighted the vital role of the wider squad, noting that a positive attitude and commitment behind the scenes are what truly drive team culture, drawing a direct parallel to school sports teams.’

#1949. New heights and same problems: How Milan stars fared in the November international break

With just a few days until the return of AC Milan action, the international break is now done. Let’s take a look at how the internationals fared.

Whether you love it or you hate it, the international break is now over and players are trickling back into Milanello. Even those who didn’t head away are only just really returning, with Ruben Amorim offering the squad a week off.

So, let’s look at what Amorim has returning, with several things to shout about…

Christian Pulisic probably leaves the break as the star of the week(s). His brace against Haiti helped secure a place in the CONCACAF Nations League semifinals, and he then rounded it off with a bicycle kick in the second leg.

After missing the penultimate international break of the season – to ensure he was fully back to fitness – he’s quickly reminded everyone of how important he can be for club and country, scoring his seventh goal of the season in only 13 games.

He’s on fire and there are no signs of him slowing down anytime soon.

You’d then have to speak about Diego Moreira, who has left the international break – somehow – with more praise than he started it with. He starred in Belgium’s 2-1 win against Turkiye and then followed that up with a goal against Italy.

It gets to a point where you run out of superlatives to describe a player and his teammates are already at that stage. Both Mark Van Bommel and Koni De Winter have called him crazy (in a good way), with the former even putting him in the same group as Kevin De Bruyne and Jeremy Doku.

He’s become a starter for the Red Devils and it’s difficult to see that changing.

In terms of the Italians, Milan had a few reasons to smile and it starts with Alphadjo Cisse. At first, it seemed he’d been wasted during the break, with Roberto Mancini not calling him up for the game against France.

However, he was given the nod for the second game and got some valuable minutes on the field. As the Rossoneri have become familiar with, he took that chance with both hands, scoring a disallowed goal and winning a penalty in a defeat to Belgium.

He’s shining with confidence currently and long may it continue.

Then, Francesco Camarda is probably at the other end of the scale. He’s clearly not got the most confidence when representing the Diavolo, but returning to the youth level, he shone like he always has.

Against Sankhoun Diawara’s France side, he was excellent. In terms of his hold-up play, finishing and just general performance, he was almost perfect, if not perfect. With a goal to round it off too, he leaves the break with a much-needed confidence boost.

Unfortunately, we can’t say the same for Goncalo Ramos. After Cristiano Ronaldo’s retirement, this was a chance for him to take the star role and prove that he’s going to be the man to ensure things keep ticking.

Instead, he left the break leaving Portugal with more questions than answers, which is a familiar feeling.

He played just shy of 150 minutes during the break and mustered just one shot. It’s not like he provided an assist or any key passes either. In other words, it’s another blank for him and it’s clearly having an effect.

Without a goal in 661 minutes, it’s no shock why the Diavolo are so heavily pursuing a striker ahead of January.

For France, it was a relatively quiet break for Mike Maignan and Adrien Rabiot. Neither performed especially well against Italy in a 3-1 loss at San Siro, though Rabiot was named as the captain for that game. Then, in the second game, Maignan was injured. However, it seems he’ll be fine for this weekend.

Not a lot to shout about for those two, but that’s not necessarily a bad thing either.

For Luka Modric, his minutes were focused in the right areas. He played 14 minutes in a nothing game against England, but was then essential in a 2-1 win against the Czech Republic, which may help them qualify for the latter stages of the Nations League.

It was another strange international break for Ardon Jashari, too. He was given no minutes against Slovenia in a 0-0 draw, but then played the full 90 minutes against Scotland, where they won 4-0. He made 76 passes from 90 touches, so he had some involvement. However, he’s still a way away from being a dictator of the team, as it was hoped he’d be.

Davide Bartesaghi, Christian Comotto and Sankhoun Diawara were all given valuable minutes during the break. Finally, Pervis Estupinan played 36 minutes over the break. He returns without any injuries and that’s all there is to really say about his past fortnight.

#1948. Two more points lost but Scott Parker’s gamble paid off | West Ham News

Just over one year ago, West Ham’s Finlay Herrick was stepping out on loan for Boreham Wood in the National League – the fifth tier of English football. A far cry from London Stadium yesterday as he replaced Mads Hermansen in goal and made his Championship debut, apparently hearing about his impending start just on the morning of the game.

And despite the first half concession from the corner, Herrick did a pretty fair job with excellent double saves later in the game and some assured glove work catching the ball – which had seemed like a lost art at times in the last couple of years.

Herrick after his unforgettable FA Cup penalty shootout debut last year

This was a massive gamble by Scott Parker which could have backfired dreadfully. With no Areola, the temptation must have been to revert to Hermansen yet the Hammers’ head coach stuck with his instinct. After the first half goal concession, Parker must have wondered – briefly – whether he’d made a huge howler.

Has Herrick done enough to keep his place? It seems Parker is dead set on replacing Hermansen so until Alphonse Areola is ‘fit and ready’ then Herrick should be prepared for more pitch time. He certainly has the ambition:

“I hope this is the start. I hope I’ve done myself justice and proved to the fans that I don’t just want to be third choice, I want to be playing, I want to get back to the Premier League and be part of that”. (whu/youtube)

Describing the competition amongst the trio of goal keepers, Herrick was quick to praise Hermansen for the encouragement and help he’s received recently, describing the three keepers as a team more than individuals fighting amongst themselves for the sole starting spot:

“There’s one goal keeper shirt and there’s three of us – but we’re like a band of brothers and we always stick together, me Mads and Fonz- no matter what. “

Difficult to believe Herrick is still only 20 – he seems to have been around West Ham’s fringes for ever- but he joined the academy at six years old and looks to have the talent to go all the way. From yesterday’s solid start, he didn’t let his manager or his team mates down and should feel rightly pretty proud of himself.

The question for Scott Parker is whether he continues between the sticks at Fratton Park on Tuesday night.

#1946. Call Me Crazy, But I’m Still Backing This West Ham Team – Here’s Why

As I left the London Stadium to a chorus of boos, I found myself desperately searching for positives from a frustrating 1-1 draw against the league’s bottom club.

The first was the performance of Alvarez. Largely cast into the shadows through the stubbornness of our former manager, he grabbed the game by the scruff of the neck. He took control, lifted the crowd, and, above all, displayed the leadership qualities this team has lacked for much of the season.

The second positive was that the statistics backed up what I’d watched unfold on the pitch. West Ham dominated possession with 79%, registered 30 shots, and recorded an xG of 3.13. The problem? Only four of those efforts were shots on target.

We gifted Preston their opening goal. It came from a calamitous mix-up, with Piroe’s flicked header looping backwards onto the crossbar before dropping kindly for Liam Lindsay to tap home from close range. It could be argued that Herrick should have been more commanding from the corner, but he made amends later with an excellent double save.

There were concerns that we wouldn’t pull one back, we did on the 60th minute, Mavropanos heading home his sixth goal in 15 league appearances this season.

“Ifs” and “buts” don’t win football matches, and as Parker said afterwards: “The overall performance suggests we should win. The fine margins of football are, and the reality is, if Tomas Soucek scores that last-minute goal, it’s probably a different interview.”

For me, I’m not going to be negative. We needed a win and we didn’t get the three points, but what I want to see now is the team build on the domination, the chance creation and the shot volume by going to Fratton Park on Tuesday and getting the job done. If we concede first there and deliver an abject performance, then and only then will there be more serious questions to ask.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

#1945. Absolutely appalling abuse for Dan Burn from Newcastle United fans after he said this

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

If you hadn’t heard of Dan Burn and somebody detailed his journey in football, there is no way you would believe it.

Santiago Munez and Goal! sounds like a very believable factual documentary in comparison.

Dan Burn one of countless kids taken on by the Newcastle United Academy but don’t make it.

In his case, it was at the age of 11 when told his dream ended there.

The rest is history. Though you would be forgiven if you double checked certain facts because they sound like the work of somebody’s very active imagination.

Dan Burn who entered the world of men’s football with Darlington at non-league level, whilst working part-time collecting shopping trolleys at ASDA.

Through grit, determination and of course ability, Dan Burn developed a very decent career for himself, playing for Fulham, Yeovil, Wigan, Birmingham and Brighton.

This career not standing out as a stellar one, but certainly a very decent life in football, with a fair few Premier League appearances amongst his 300+ games across the years.

Then just over three months ahead of his 30th birthday, Dan Burn got the call that was going to change his life forever.

Inheriting a desperate mid-season relegation fight when taking the Newcastle United job in November 2021, two months later Eddie Howe was looking to bring in ready to play Premier League experienced players to avoid instant disaster for the then new Newcastle United owners.

Kieran Trippier, Chris Wood and Matt Targett arrived at St James’ Park in January 2022, with Brighton reluctantly allowing Dan Burn to join that trio for a reported £13m transfer fee. Eddie Howe and the Newcastle United owners were ridiculed by many journalists, pundits and fans of other clubs. Tagged as the ‘richest’ club owners in world football and yet they and their manager thought Dan Burn was the kind of signing they needed. Hilarious. Bruno Guimaraes also arrived in that same transfer window but he was aimed at the longer-term, new to the Premier League it would be March 2022 before he started a game for NUFC, by which point United were well on their way to safety with Burn, Targett and Wood playing key roles in that, Kieran Trippier also started well but very quickly picked up a significant injury and only returned at the very end of that season.

With relegation avoided, Eddie Howe brought in the exciting young Dutch left-footed central defender Sven Botman, who when he was 20 turning 21 played a key role in a stunning Ligue 1 title success for Lille.

With the summer 2022 signing of Botman, I don’t think any Newcastle fan would have been surprised if Dan Burn had then ended up becoming a squad player. Instead he became a player that Eddie Howe picked every match with very few exceptions. Matt Targett picked up an injury very early that 2022-23 season and Dan Burn was moved to left-back.

The back five that played almost every Premier League match that 2022-23 season was Pope, Trippier, Schar, Botman Burn.

The ‘experts’ couldn’t believe it, Eddie Howe and Newcastle United finished fourth in the Premier League and qualified for the Champions League, plus NUFC got to their first Wembley final in 24 years.

That success was massively built on an astonishing defensive record.

Manchester City won the 2022-23 Premier League title only conceding 33 goals in the 38 league matches, this Newcastle United five matched that low goals conceded total. In the six Carabao Cup matches that got United to Wembley, only two goals were conceded across the half dozen matches.

Eddie Howe had created something very special at Newcastle United and Dan Burn was one of the first names on the team sheet, whether playing in the centre of defence or left-back.

Dan Burn finally living the Newcastle United dream in his 30s.

He was somebody the fans could really relate to, many of us kidding ourselves that if only things had worked out a little differently, that could have been you or me instead of Dan Burn in a Newcastle United shirt. That wasn’t the reality of course but that is how Dan Burn makes you feel. That he is a Newcastle United fan who by that sheer grit and determination is playing for NUFC, rather than watching them.

We have had many other homegrown heroes, many in my lifetime, but Alan Shearer had this incredible talent for scoring goals that elevated him above all others in the Premier League, whilst Peter Beardsley and Paul Gascoigne just had incredible talent that for me matches any player I have ever seen play football for any club or country.

As for Dan Burn, he has continued to be phenomenal in the colours of Newcastle United.

The 2023-24 was one of the worst ever for Newcastle United injuries, all but mission impossible for Eddie Howe and his small squad to lose so many players so often, plus the disastrous Sandro Tonali suspension. With the squad hit by so many injuries, when Dan Burn picked up a serious one to his back, he came back far earlier than the medical staff wanted him to because the manager, team and fans needed him. Newcastle United still managed 60 EPL points that 2023-24 season and came so close to qualifying from their Champions League group which was as tough as it could possibly be. One opponent reached the final and another the semi-final. United were cheated in Paris out of a famous win that would have led to them qualifying instead of PSG. In the stunning 4-1 home win over PSG, Dan Burn was immense at the back and scored THAT goal.

The finances meant Newcastle United didn’t buy any new first team players in summer 2024 and indeed a PSR crisis that had to be dealt with in June 2024 meant Elliot Anderson and Yankuba Minteh were sold. Dan Burn and his Newcastle United team-mates reacted by producing the most successful season in living memory for most of us. Another Champions League qualification. Oh..and a trophy. The unforgettable sight of Dan Burn scoring the best headed goal Wembley (new or old) has ever seen. Burn one of United’s very best players that magical day, a trophy finally lifted on 16 March 2025.

The 2025-26 season proved far too much for a still too small Newcastle United squad to cope with a 58 game season, especially as injuries piled up once again. Including Dan Burn the victim of a cowardly challenge during the away derby mix, the Geordie warrior wanted to try and play on, even though it was later discovered he’d punctured a lung and broken a rib. As always, his commitment was immense during such a challenging season.

The perfect choice to be the new Newcastle United captain, injury delayed his 2026-27 season kicking off. No surprise that things significantly improved at the back when Dan Burn was able to start in the Premier League. After conceding 14 goals in the opening seven Premier League matches, the next three saw only two conceded (against Palace, Everton and Fulham). Then Dan Burn leading Newcastle United to Saturday’s comeback draw against an Arsenal side that had won nine of their opening ten EPL matches.

Dan Burn getting absolutely appalling abuse from Newcastle United fans

In recent days a video has circulated online, Dan Burn stopped and asked for one of those one minute video interviews, where random questions are fired and only need a name as the answer.

I’m not sure when the video interview happened but my guess is that Dan Burn was stopped as he went into the Newcastle United Foundation dinner last week, which was to raise funds for the charity and to celebrate local achievers.

These are the questions and answers, I have changed the order in which they were asked, see if you can guess which one has prompted the abuse aimed at Dan Burn.

Best player played against – Ronaldo Funniest player – Jacob Murphy Best leader – Jordan Henderson Best finisher – Harry Kane Best on a night out – Lewis Dunk Best player you have played with – Alexander Isak Biggest prankster – David Perkins Toughest played against – Adama Traore Most famous person on your phone – Sam Fender

It is important to point out that those Newcastle United fans giving Dan Burn this appalling abuse are only some Newcastle United fans, not all NUFC fans.

Of course I don’t know if every single one of them who are giving abuse is a Newcastle fan but certainly many of them are. As it is online you can see that they regularly post comments about NUFC and I have no doubt these people are Newcastle fans.

So just in case you were still wondering which answer has prompted all of this abuse, it is Dan Burn saying Alexander Isak is the best player he has played with.

Apparently this is an unforgivable crime, at least for some Newcastle United fans.

That this then justifies saying what a useless football player Dan Burn is AND far far worse, these fans aiming abuse at him as a person, his character.

Everybody is of course entitled to their own opinion BUT I can’t even attempt to get my head around why anyone would have this opinion AND even worse, be desperate to tell everyone else.

The best thing about social media is that everybody can now have their say.

The worst thing about social media is that everybody can now have their say.

I have no doubt that if Dan Burn sees these abusive comments he will just brush them to one side. It is just a fact that people get abuse online, especially if they are famous.

It depresses me the way many Newcastle United fans go on at times. One match, even one moment in a match, can see some Newcastle United fans giving one of our players ridiculous levels of criticism, even if they have done incredible things for the club and fans. It is like those fans who now want us to believe that Eddie Howe simply got lucky with the success he brought to NUFC, that he just stumbled along and it as all down to others why Newcastle United were suddenly winning football matches, getting to Wembley, playing in the Champions League and….winning a trophy.

This abuse for Dan Burn though, it really does my head in.

Why would any Newcastle United fan think it is appropriate?

To me, Dan Burn represents everything that is positive about Newcastle United and the people of our region.

If you asked him to run through a brick wall for Newcastle United, he would ask which one he should run through first.

Dan Burn makes me proud to be a Newcastle United fan, proud to be a Geordie.

He has been brilliant for Newcastle United, brought us so much joy, whilst off the pitch he is the same.

Countless charity events and also brave enough to talk about his mental health struggles of the past, in order to help others.

Dan Burn names the BEST player he’s ever played with 🤝🔥 https://t.co/4eqSbEhB6a

— All Out Football (@ItsAllOutFooty) November 17, 2026

Nobody is above criticism but I would love to see some Newcastle United fans just tone it down a bit. Instead of unleashing hate aimed at some of the best amongst us, have a think before giving a reaction.
